label: fiction
title: The Alibi That Spoke
setting: The present-day fictional state of Orinth, after security officers prevented an attack during First Councillor Ilyra Senn’s public address on flood recovery.
charge: attempting a terrorist assassination of the head of government
elements: The accused intended to kill the fictional head of government.
The accused took an act that went beyond mere preparation.
The accused intended the attack to intimidate the public or coerce the fictional government for an ideological purpose.
hook: A live call bearing Corin Vale’s face clears a delivery into First Councillor Ilyra Senn’s venue. At the same minute, Corin is speaking before a luncheon audience elsewhere. The call is synthetic. The jury must decide who controlled what happened next.

accused.human: Corin Vale, 39, is a civic-media consultant who teaches schools and public offices how synthetic images can undermine trust.
accused.if_guilty: Any sentence is a matter for the judge after the verdict and must play no part in the jury’s decision.

prosecution.speaker: pc
prosecution.text: The prosecution alleges Corin Vale acted as a principal: Corin personally sent the activation command after arranging a synthetic authorization call and a visible luncheon appearance. You’ll hear how the delivery entered, who could access the studio project, and what a separate hardware token recorded. The prosecution says those facts prove an intended political killing, not merely careless media work.

defence.speaker: dc
defence.text: The defence says the synthetic call and studio archive identify no operator. Corin’s collaborators shared the source recordings, administrator account, draft, and stage bag containing the token. The activation record proves a token was used, not whose hand used it. Jori Dane changed accounts after receiving immunity. Decide whether suspicion about a strange demonstration can identify a principal beyond reasonable doubt.

prosecution.speaker: pc
prosecution.text: The shared studio archive alone would not be enough. Start instead with Corin’s own instruction to Jori, then the hardware token: it was registered to Corin, recovered from Corin’s bag, and physically confirmed during Corin’s unobserved greenroom interval. Add the risk scenario Corin admits writing and the command sent seconds later. The prosecution says Corin personally crossed from preparation to attempt.

defence.speaker: dc
defence.text: The prosecution cannot turn possession into identity. Daro Quill carried the stage bag and knew the token’s ordinary approval routine; the greenroom side entrance was not filmed. The shared project log cannot distinguish four users. Jori first denied any instruction, and Corin’s draft describes a safety demonstration, not an attack. If another authorised collaborator could have used these materials and the token, you cannot be sure Corin sent the command.

epilogue: Ilyra Senn later completed the flood-recovery address from a smaller civic hall and commissioned an independent review of synthetic authorisation at public venues. Jori Dane left events work after acknowledging the inspection bypass. Corin Vale’s teaching materials remained sealed with the trial exhibits while former students argued over whether the lessons had been misused or misunderstood. The venue replaced face-and-voice approvals with two-person confirmation, and the luncheon recording continued to circulate as a reminder that a genuine appearance can coexist with a false one.

beats.speaker: w3

turns.speaker: pc
turns.text: What was your responsibility at Ilyra Senn’s address?

turns.speaker: w3
turns.text: Every private delivery needed inspection and a second officer’s approval.

turns.speaker: pc
turns.text: What happened at two o’clock?

turns.speaker: w3
turns.text: A live call showed Corin saying a controlled media-test package was expected and giving our advance code. I accepted it and bypassed the second approval.

beats.text: What was your responsibility at Ilyra Senn’s address? Every private delivery needed inspection and a second officer’s approval. What happened at two o’clock? A live call showed Corin saying a controlled media-test package was expected and giving our advance code. I accepted it and bypassed the second approval.
beats.reveal_note: Jori personally received the call and breached the venue rule. The evidence established how the delivery entered, not who created the synthetic caller.

beats.speaker: w1

turns.speaker: pc
turns.text: How did you preserve what the search found?

turns.speaker: w1
turns.text: I led the search, photographed the sealed package where it stood, and recorded every transfer to the protective laboratory.

turns.speaker: pc
turns.text: What did the examination and provider record establish?

turns.speaker: w1
turns.text: The package contained a destructive device. At 2:06, an activation command was sent, but our isolation system prevented it from reaching the device.

beats.text: How did you preserve what the search found? I led the search, photographed the sealed package where it stood, and recorded every transfer to the protective laboratory. What did the examination and provider record establish? The package contained a destructive device. At 2:06, an activation command was sent, but our isolation system prevented it from reaching the device.
beats.reveal_note: The documented scene, custody, examination, and provider record proved an attempted activation beyond mere preparation. They did not identify its sender.

beats.speaker: w1

turns.speaker: dc
turns.text: You found no fingerprint or biological material from Corin on the package?

turns.speaker: w1
turns.text: That’s correct.

turns.speaker: dc
turns.text: And the first provider certificate named an account, not a human sender?

turns.speaker: w1
turns.text: Yes. It showed the activation account and time. We needed separate evidence about who controlled the account and its hardware token.

beats.text: You found no fingerprint or biological material from Corin on the package? That’s correct. And the first provider certificate named an account, not a human sender? Yes. It showed the activation account and time. We needed separate evidence about who controlled the account and its hardware token.
beats.reveal_note: The investigator accepted both attribution gaps. Neither the physical device nor the account name could identify Corin without independent control evidence.

beats.speaker: w2

turns.speaker: pc
turns.text: What material did you examine from the authorization call?

turns.speaker: w2
turns.text: I received the provider’s original stream under a custodian certificate, verified its hash, and analysed its image and sound tracks.

turns.speaker: pc
turns.text: What could you conclude?

turns.speaker: w2
turns.text: The face and voice were synthetically generated. The finished stream contains no reliable marker identifying its creator.

beats.text: What material did you examine from the authorization call? I received the provider’s original stream under a custodian certificate, verified its hash, and analysed its image and sound tracks. What could you conclude? The face and voice were synthetically generated. The finished stream contains no reliable marker identifying its creator.
beats.reveal_note: The authenticated expert analysis proved the call was synthetic. It did not prove that Corin was framed or identify the creator.

beats.speaker: w2

turns.speaker: dc
turns.text: Who could access the Second Presence source archive?

turns.speaker: w2
turns.text: Corin, two employees, and contractor Daro Quill.

turns.speaker: dc
turns.text: Could its activity log distinguish those four people?

turns.speaker: w2
turns.text: Not for the relevant work. They used one administrator credential. The forensic image and hashes preserve the files accurately, but the shared login cannot identify which authorised user created the call project.

beats.text: Who could access the Second Presence source archive? Corin, two employees, and contractor Daro Quill. Could its activity log distinguish those four people? Not for the relevant work. They used one administrator credential. The forensic image and hashes preserve the files accurately, but the shared login cannot identify which authorised user created the call project.
beats.reveal_note: The authenticated archive proved the project existed but could not attribute its relevant activity among four authorised collaborators. That was a genuine limit, not a speculative possibility.

beats.speaker: w2

turns.speaker: pc
turns.text: What relevant material was in that preserved archive?

turns.speaker: w2
turns.text: A project called Second Presence used recent recordings of Corin and included the unusual phrase, “Proceed with the test although I’m on stage.”

turns.speaker: pc
turns.text: What happened to the project after the call?

turns.speaker: w2
turns.text: The shared administrator account queued deletion for 2:13. The archive proves timing and source material, but not which authorised user set the queue.

beats.text: What relevant material was in that preserved archive? A project called Second Presence used recent recordings of Corin and included the unusual phrase, “Proceed with the test although I’m on stage.” What happened to the project after the call? The shared administrator account queued deletion for 2:13. The archive proves timing and source material, but not which authorised user set the queue.
beats.reveal_note: The project closely matched the synthetic call and its timing. Shared access prevented the archive from proving Corin personally operated it.

beats.speaker: w3

turns.speaker: pc
turns.text: What, if anything, did Corin tell you the evening before the address?

turns.speaker: w3
turns.text: Corin said, “My second voice will approve a controlled delivery at two. Use code Vale-four and don’t hold it for the second officer.”

turns.speaker: pc
turns.text: Did Corin describe violence or a political purpose?

turns.speaker: w3
turns.text: No. I thought it was an authorised media-security test.

beats.text: What, if anything, did Corin tell you the evening before the address? Corin said, “My second voice will approve a controlled delivery at two. Use code Vale-four and don’t hold it for the second officer.” Did Corin describe violence or a political purpose? No. I thought it was an authorised media-security test.
beats.reveal_note: If accepted, Jori’s account connected Corin to the planned synthetic approval and inspection bypass. It did not establish what Corin believed the package contained.

beats.speaker: w3

turns.speaker: dc
turns.text: You first denied any advance instruction from Corin?

turns.speaker: w3
turns.text: Yes. I’d broken the inspection rule and panicked.

turns.speaker: dc
turns.text: You gave this account after receiving limited immunity?

turns.speaker: w3
turns.text: Yes, for the bypass.

turns.speaker: dc
turns.text: And Daro Quill also knew the demonstration schedule and delivery code?

turns.speaker: w3
turns.text: Daro knew the schedule and had seen the code sheet. I never heard Corin discuss an attack.

beats.text: You first denied any advance instruction from Corin? Yes. I’d broken the inspection rule and panicked. You gave this account after receiving limited immunity? Yes, for the bypass. And Daro Quill also knew the demonstration schedule and delivery code? Daro knew the schedule and had seen the code sheet. I never heard Corin discuss an attack.
beats.reveal_note: Jori’s changed account and immunity were material credibility concerns. Daro’s independent knowledge also prevented Jori’s evidence from proving exclusive control.

beats.speaker: w1

turns.speaker: pc
turns.text: What separate record linked the activation command to Corin?

turns.speaker: w1
turns.text: The provider certified that its fresh challenge was confirmed at 2:06 by Corin’s registered, non-exportable hardware token. We seized that token from Corin’s stage bag with its seals intact.

turns.speaker: pc
turns.text: Where was the bag then?

turns.speaker: w1
turns.text: Custodian-certified venue footage shows Corin taking it into a greenroom at 2:04 and emerging alone at 2:07.

beats.text: What separate record linked the activation command to Corin? The provider certified that its fresh challenge was confirmed at 2:06 by Corin’s registered, non-exportable hardware token. We seized that token from Corin’s stage bag with its seals intact. Where was the bag then? Custodian-certified venue footage shows Corin taking it into a greenroom at 2:04 and emerging alone at 2:07.
beats.reveal_note: The independently certified provider, seizure, and venue records put Corin’s physical token with Corin during the fresh confirmation window. This was the prosecution’s central attribution evidence.

beats.speaker: w2

turns.speaker: dc
turns.text: Does the hardware token identify the person who touched it?

turns.speaker: w2
turns.text: No. It proves physical confirmation by that token, not a fingerprint.

turns.speaker: dc
turns.text: Could Daro have prepared the confirmation before Corin entered the greenroom?

turns.speaker: w2
turns.text: Not this challenge. The provider issued it at 2:06 and it expired thirty seconds later. Someone near the token then had to confirm it.

beats.text: Does the hardware token identify the person who touched it? No. It proves physical confirmation by that token, not a fingerprint. Could Daro have prepared the confirmation before Corin entered the greenroom? Not this challenge. The provider issued it at 2:06 and it expired thirty seconds later. Someone near the token then had to confirm it.
beats.reveal_note: The expert resisted overclaiming identity but excluded advance use. The token had to be physically confirmed during Corin’s unobserved greenroom interval.

beats.speaker: acc

turns.speaker: dc
turns.text: What was Second Presence meant to be?

turns.speaker: acc
turns.text: A proposal for an approved security demonstration. Four of us built scenarios and source material.

turns.speaker: dc
turns.text: Why did your draft mention frightening a crowd and pressuring the council?

turns.speaker: acc
turns.text: It described the risk we wanted officials to prevent: a borrowed face causing panic and pushing authority toward emergency controls. It wasn’t an instruction to attack anyone.

beats.text: What was Second Presence meant to be? A proposal for an approved security demonstration. Four of us built scenarios and source material. Why did your draft mention frightening a crowd and pressuring the council? It described the risk we wanted officials to prevent: a borrowed face causing panic and pushing authority toward emergency controls. It wasn’t an instruction to attack anyone.
beats.reveal_note: Corin admitted writing the risk scenario and gave it a credible professional meaning. The writing was ambiguous and could not operate as a confession.

beats.speaker: acc

turns.speaker: pc
turns.text: You wrote that a public failure could force the council to transfer authentication power to a civic network?

turns.speaker: acc
turns.text: Yes, as a warning about what panic could do.

turns.speaker: pc
turns.text: At 2:06, your registered token was inside the bag you had taken into the greenroom?

turns.speaker: acc
turns.text: It should have been. Daro carried that bag earlier and knew the approval routine. The side entrance wasn’t filmed. I didn’t send the command.

beats.text: You wrote that a public failure could force the council to transfer authentication power to a civic network? Yes, as a warning about what panic could do. At 2:06, your registered token was inside the bag you had taken into the greenroom? It should have been. Daro carried that bag earlier and knew the approval routine. The side entrance wasn’t filmed. I didn’t send the command.
beats.reveal_note: Corin accepted authorship, possession, and the policy consequence described in the draft while denying criminal use. The side-entrance possibility remained a real defence point, not proof that Daro entered.

beats.speaker: judge
beats.text: The parties agree that no Orinth office, venue officer, or protective agency authorised a Second Presence test for that day. Corin’s earlier written proposal had not been approved, and neither Jori nor the second inspection officer received an exercise notice. You may also accept that the intercepted package was not a training item. These facts do not identify who sent the activation command.
beats.reveal_note: The agreed records answered the claim of an authorised exercise but expressly left personal attribution to the other evidence.

beats.speaker: judge
beats.text: The prosecution alleges Corin personally sent the activation command. It is not enough that Corin owned the project, wrote a risk scenario, or may have helped someone else. You must be sure Corin sent the command intending to kill Ilyra Senn and intending public intimidation or government coercion for an ideological purpose. If you are not sure of every element beyond reasonable doubt, your verdict must be Not Guilty.
beats.reveal_note: The direction confines liability to Corin’s alleged personal activation and prevents project ownership, ambiguous writing, or another person’s conduct from replacing proof.

twist: The authors’ intended resolution is Guilty on principal liability, not because Corin owned a synthetic-media studio. The central inference is that Corin’s non-exportable token was freshly confirmed while certified footage placed the token and Corin together during the activation window; Jori’s advance instruction and the unapproved risk scenario support intent. The strongest reasonable opposing interpretation is that Daro used shared project access and briefly reached the bag through the unfilmed side entrance, while Corin’s writing described a legitimate safety demonstration.

jurors.label: Juror 2 — Anya
jurors.persona: Anya’s first reaction is that a stolen face must mean a frame, but she can revise a vivid impression.

agree: The fake call could be a frame, and four people could use the source archive. Isn’t that real doubt?
pushback: But the fake call isn’t the activation command. What do we do with the token in Corin’s bag?
concede: Wait—the fresh token challenge changes my first reaction. The copied face isn’t the only identity evidence.
burden_drift: I keep wanting Corin to explain every studio file because the work feels suspicious.
burden_correct: No, shared access means the prosecution needs a separate link to Corin personally.
final: I stopped treating the fake face as the answer and decided on the token evidence.

jurors.label: Juror 3 — Bex
jurors.persona: Bex focuses on who gave each instruction and refuses to merge Jori’s conduct with Corin’s.

agree: Jori says Corin supplied the exact code and told her to skip the second officer. That matters.
pushback: I don’t trust Jori’s later memory on its own. What backs it up?
concede: The token record is separate from Jori and points to Corin during the command window.
burden_drift: Jori broke the rule, and I catch myself asking Corin to prove Jori acted alone.
burden_correct: Let’s keep them separate: the prosecution must prove Corin’s own activation.
final: I relied on Corin’s personal command, not guilt by association with Jori.

jurors.label: Juror 4 — Cora
jurors.persona: Cora will not let the seriousness of the prevented attack lower the standard or blur personal identity.

agree: The attack was real and grave. That still doesn’t tell us whose hand confirmed the token.
pushback: An ambiguous safety draft cannot repair weak identity evidence.
concede: I accept the timing is unusually tight: Corin, the bag, the fresh challenge, and the command all meet at 2:06.
burden_drift: The avoided harm makes an uncertain inference feel easier than it should.
burden_correct: Every element still needs proof beyond reasonable doubt, including Corin’s personal act.
final: For me, the independently certified timing finally crossed the burden.

jurors.label: Juror 5 — Dev
jurors.persona: Dev begins with the shared-access defence and changes only if another record attributes the decisive act.

agree: The administrator log genuinely can’t distinguish four authorised people. We shouldn’t pretend it can.
pushback: Shared project access answers the call project, but does it answer the separate token?
concede: I’ve changed my view. The fresh challenge prevents Daro from preparing the activation earlier.
burden_drift: A pile of matching records can make me overlook which one actually identifies a person.
burden_correct: The prosecution needs a trace to Corin’s own act, not just to Corin’s business.
final: The project remained shared; the activation token and timing did not.

jurors.label: Juror 6 — Eren
jurors.persona: Eren keeps the discussion on Corin’s alleged personal act and asks the room to name its source.

agree: We agree an activation was attempted. Can we now focus on who personally confirmed it?
pushback: The draft speaks about a risk. Where’s the proof that Corin wanted that risk to happen?
concede: The token timing answers identity for me; the unapproved device and admitted policy goal answer intent together.
burden_drift: We’re drifting toward asking Corin to identify whoever used the side entrance.
burden_correct: Corin doesn’t have to name another operator. The prosecution has to make us sure it was Corin.
final: I checked the personal act first, then intent, instead of letting the event decide for me.

jurors.label: Juror 7 — Fia
jurors.persona: Fia is strongly influenced by Corin’s simultaneous luncheon appearance until the room separates call creation from activation.

agree: Corin is onstage during the fake call. I know that’s not a complete alibi, but it still matters.
pushback: Are we sure the person in the greenroom was alone, or only that the hallway camera saw one person?
concede: I was letting the luncheon image control everything. Corin could be onstage at two and use the token at 2:06.
burden_drift: Corin’s expertise makes me want proof that no collaborator copied anything.
burden_correct: That’s wrong. The prosecution must prove Corin used this token for this command.
final: The public appearance didn’t answer what happened six minutes later.

jurors.label: Juror 8 — Garen
jurors.persona: Garen distinguishes the shared synthetic-media work from the later human decision to activate the device.

agree: The expert proved the call archive was shared. The activation token is a different system and a different question.
pushback: A shared login means we can’t attribute the project activity to Corin. I won’t pretend otherwise.
concede: I accept that the token doesn’t record a fingerprint, but the fresh challenge sharply limits who could use it.
burden_drift: Technical complexity can make Corin’s innocent explanation feel like a duty.
burden_correct: We should rely on proved limits and links, not demand a complete production history from Corin.
final: I treated the project attribution as unresolved and the activation attribution as proved.

jurors.label: Juror 9 — Hali
jurors.persona: Hali distrusts immunity evidence and asks whether independent records confirm the precise part Jori added later.

agree: Jori changed the story after immunity, and Daro knew the code too. We can’t skip that.
pushback: Maybe Jori is telling the truth now, but which record confirms Corin gave the instruction?
concede: The token doesn’t prove Jori’s words, but it independently connects Corin to the later command.
burden_drift: I almost asked Corin to prove Jori and Daro acted together. That isn’t Corin’s burden.
burden_correct: We have to test Jori against independent evidence, not against Corin’s ability to solve the case.
final: I used Jori cautiously and reached identity through the separate token record.

jurors.label: Juror 10 — Ivo
jurors.persona: Ivo reacts strongly to the inspection bypass and has to correct a tendency to treat ownership as control.

agree: Jori says Corin set up the bypass before the fake call. That’s a direct accusation.
pushback: Daro knew the code and carried the bag. Why isn’t that enough for doubt?
concede: The 2:06 challenge wasn’t sitting around for Daro to prepare. That’s the point I was missing.
burden_drift: Corin owned the token, so part of me says Corin should name who else touched it.
burden_correct: No—ownership isn’t enough. The prosecution must prove the specific criminal use.
final: The narrow confirmation window, not ownership alone, decided identity for me.

jurors.label: Juror 11 — Jessa
jurors.persona: Jessa starts undecided and speaks cautiously while comparing the shared archive with the separate token records.

agree: I think the shared account leaves the call creator open. Four authorised users is not a theoretical possibility.
pushback: But could Daro really reach the token during that thirty-second challenge? I’m struggling with that.
concede: The timing is specific enough for me: the token, Corin, and the activation window line up independently.
burden_drift: Corin’s expertise makes the defence explanation feel like Corin’s job to prove.
burden_correct: Expertise is only context. We still need a specific connection to the command.
final: I kept the call attribution open and decided the separate activation attribution.

jurors.label: Juror 12 — Kellan
jurors.persona: Kellan keeps the prevented harm visible while insisting that intervention does not lower the burden on identity or intent.

agree: The device was placed and activation was attempted. Security intervention doesn’t turn that back into preparation.
pushback: A prevented death still requires proof of who acted and what that person intended.
concede: The token timing identifies Corin for me; the unapproved test and admitted pressure scenario give the act its purpose.
burden_drift: Knowing what almost happened makes me impatient with the alternative explanation.
burden_correct: Prevention doesn’t lower the burden of proving Corin’s identity and intent.
final: I separated the real danger from the proof, then found both the act and intent established.
